curatorBrief.title: Welcome to the Counting Safari!
curatorBrief.intent: Introduce kindergarten learners to counting real objects up to 10 using one-to-one touch correspondence and recognizing the written numerals 1 through 10 in standard order.

components.title: Touch and Count Safari Animals
components.intent: Guide kindergarteners to count up to 10 friendly safari objects (such as playful bears, apples, and stars) by touching each item one by one with spoken count confirmation to build one-to-one correspondence.

components.title: Fill the Ten-Frame
components.intent: Engage students in placing counters into a single ten-frame to represent counted amounts from 1 to 10, establishing strong visual cardinality and subitizing anchors.

components.title: Hands-On Toy Counter Hunt
components.intent: Provide a fun screen-free family activity where children collect up to 10 small household items (blocks, spoons, or toy cars), line them up, and touch-count each one out loud.

objectiveBlocks.objectiveText: Identify written numbers from 1 to 10 in order

components.title: Explore the 1 to 10 Number Track
components.intent: Introduce the standard order of numbers from 1 to 10 using an interactive linear grid, highlighting each written numeral in sequence from left to right.

components.title: Number Train Order Game
components.intent: Have students fill missing numerals and place scrambled number cards from 1 to 10 in proper numerical sequence along a colorful train track.

components.title: Trace the Numbers 1 to 10
components.intent: Help students connect the visual form and sequence of numerals 1 to 10 by tracing the dotted paths of each digit in order.

finalAssessment.intent: Assess students across both objectives: counting groups of up to 10 items accurately with one-to-one correspondence and identifying/ordering written numerals from 1 to 10.

hook.content: Imagine you are getting ready for a fun picnic with your teddy bears, and you need to bring exactly enough apples for each friend. How do you make sure you have the right amount without guessing?

bigIdea.statement: Every object gets one number, and the last number we say tells us the total amount.
bigIdea.whyItMatters: Counting helps us share toys, set the table, and figure out how many things we have all around us every day!

mindset.encouragement: Sometimes it is easy to count an item twice or skip one by accident—that happens to everyone! Just take a deep breath, slow down, and touch each object gently as you go.
mindset.growthTip: Use your finger to point right at each object while you count so you never lose your place.

data.title: The Great 10-Item Toy Parade
data.subject: Math
data.overview: Turn everyday household treasures into an exciting marching parade! In this hands-on math activity, learners collect up to 10 small objects, line them up on a parade route, and practice touch-counting out loud. Children discover that pairing each physical tap with a number word is the secret to counting accurately every time.
learningObjectives: Demonstrate one-to-one correspondence by touching exactly one object for each number word spoken from 1 to 10.
Count aloud a set of up to 10 aligned objects in correct sequence without skipping or repeating items.
Identify cardinality by recognizing that the last number counted represents the total quantity of items in the group.

steps.title: Go on a Treasure Hunt
steps.instruction: Grab your collection basket and explore your room with an adult helper. Find up to 10 small, safe objects you would like to invite to your counting parade.
steps.tip: Choose items that can easily sit flat on a table or floor without rolling away instantly.

steps.title: Set the Parade Route
steps.instruction: Stick a strip of tape or stretch a piece of yarn along the floor or table to make a straight path for your parade.

checkpoint.question: Is your parade line flat and long enough for your objects to stand side by side?

steps.title: Line Up the Marchers
steps.instruction: Place your collected objects along the parade line one by one, from left to right, leaving a little finger-space between each item.
steps.tip: Leaving space between items prevents your counting finger from touching two objects at the same time.

steps.title: Touch and Count Out Loud
steps.instruction: Start at the far left. Gently touch the first object with your pointing finger and say 'One!' Move your finger to touch the next object and say 'Two!' Continue touching each item and saying the next number until you reach the end.

checkpoint.question: How many items did you count in your parade from start to finish?

steps.scienceNote: Touching each item as you say its number name is called one-to-one correspondence. It gives your eyes, hands, and voice a chance to work as a team so nothing gets missed or double-counted.

steps.title: Make Number Station Cards
steps.instruction: Work with your helper to write numbers 1 through 10 on your small paper squares. Match each number card by placing it directly in front of the corresponding toy along your line.

checkpoint.question: Does the number on the very last card match the total number of toys in your parade?

steps.scienceNote: The final number counted tells the total amount of the whole group. In mathematics, this principle is called cardinality.

steps.title: Scramble and Recount
steps.instruction: Mix up your toys and place them back on the parade line in a totally different order, then touch-count them again to check your total.
steps.tip: Notice that even when the items swap spots, the total number of items stays the same as long as none were removed or added.

reflectionPrompts.question: What helped your fingers and voice stay together while you were counting your parade?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Demonstrate one-to-one correspondence by touching exactly one object for each number word spoken from 1 to 10.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Think about whether going slowly or leaving spaces between toys made it easier to keep track.

reflectionPrompts.question: When you reached the last toy and said the number out loud, how did that tell you how many toys you had altogether?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Identify cardinality by recognizing that the last number counted represents the total quantity of items in the group.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Think about why you did not need to recount from the start to know the total size of the group.

reflectionPrompts.question: Where else around your house could you make a parade of 10 things to count?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Count aloud a set of up to 10 aligned objects in correct sequence without skipping or repeating items.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Look at things like books on a low shelf, shoes near the door, or plastic cups in the kitchen.

documentationPrompt.instruction: Take a photo looking down at your complete parade route showing all 10 objects lined up next to their matching number cards.
documentationPrompt.suggestedCaption: I marched 10 [type of objects] in my counting parade! My favorite item at station number [favorite number] was the [favorite object].

extensions.title: The Mystery Sneak
extensions.description: Have your child cover their eyes while a helper removes 1 or 2 items from the parade. The child touch-counts the line again to find the new total and guess how many items sneaked away.

extensions.title: Sort and Count Two Teams
extensions.description: Divide your 10 objects into two groups based on an attribute (such as hard vs. soft, or items with wheels vs. items without wheels). Count each smaller group separately and determine which team has more.

safetyNotes: Adult helper recommended to supervise the treasure hunt and support number writing.
Ensure all collected objects are larger than 1.5 inches to eliminate choking hazards, especially if younger siblings are present.
Keep parade routes away from high-traffic hallways and stairs to prevent tripping.

problems.question: What number comes right after 4 when you count?
problems.rationale: When we count out loud in order, we say 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The number that comes right after 4 is 5. 3 comes before 4, and 6 comes after 5.
problems.teachingNote: Have children practice reciting number sequences starting from different numbers, or use fingers and physical counters to reinforce forward counting order.
successCriteria: Identify the number that comes next in a forward counting sequence up to 10
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: Touch and count each star: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐.
problems.rationale: When we touch and count each star one by one, we say one, two, three, four, and five. The last number we count tells us how many stars there are in all. That means there are five stars.
problems.teachingNote: Encourage young learners to practice one-to-one correspondence by pointing directly to each object from left to right as they say each number word aloud.
successCriteria: Count up to 5 objects using one-to-one correspondence.
Demonstrate the cardinality principle by identifying the total count of a set.
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.statement: If you have 7 apples and count them one by one, the last number you say is 7.
problems.rationale: This statement is true because of the cardinality principle of counting, which means the last number name said tells the total number of objects counted. When you touch and count each apple in order from one to seven, the final count of seven represents the total amount of apples.
problems.teachingNote: Reinforce that children do not need to restart counting from one after reaching the final object; the last number spoken is the total.
successCriteria: Understand that the last number said represents the total amount of counted objects
Count a set of objects up to 10 accurately
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: Which number matches five yellow stars?
problems.rationale: The numeral 5 represents a group of five objects, such as five yellow stars. When we count from one up to five, the symbol 5 tells us the total amount. The numbers 2 and 4 represent smaller groups.
problems.teachingNote: Have students count on their fingers or tap five times as they connect the spoken count to the numeral symbol 5.
successCriteria: Match a spoken quantity of objects to its written numeral up to 10
